cvFormats.name: High-school student reference format
cvFormats.summary: An anonymized educational format with fictional example bullets. It is not a real person’s CV and is not ready to submit unchanged.
cvFormats.goalAdvice: Prioritize relevant education and projects, with clear status and evidence rather than senior-level employment expectations.

sections.name: Summary
sections.why: State your direction and the evidence relevant to this application.
sections.example: Fictional educational example: engineering learner developing reproducible data analysis and technical communication through a documented public-data project.

sections.name: Education
sections.why: Include the qualification, institution and dates you can verify.
sections.example: Use your actual school or degree, institution, status and dates; do not imply a completed qualification while still enrolled.

sections.name: Relevant coursework
sections.why: Select courses that explain preparation for the role or programme.
sections.example: List completed or clearly marked in-progress courses and connect one to a project artifact.

sections.name: Technical skills
sections.why: Name methods you can demonstrate, with evidence.
sections.example: Fictional example: calibration analysis demonstrated in an annotated notebook with residual checks.

sections.name: Software and tools
sections.why: Explain what you used a tool to accomplish.
sections.example: Fictional example: Python and a version-controlled notebook used to clean public data and reproduce a figure.

sections.name: Laboratory / practical skills
sections.why: Only include techniques actually practised under appropriate supervision.
sections.example: If no laboratory experience exists, describe desk-based work honestly instead of inventing equipment access.

sections.name: Projects
sections.why: Show the question, your contribution, method and result or limitation.
sections.example: Fictional example: compared published alloy data, checked units and presented a materials-selection tradeoff.

sections.name: Research
sections.why: Distinguish a literature review, coursework and supervised original research.
sections.example: Fictional example: built a cited evidence table and identified inconsistent measurement methods; no claim of publication.

sections.name: Internships
sections.why: Name real responsibilities and dates; identify your own contribution.
sections.example: If you have no internship, omit this section and expand a relevant project or volunteering contribution.

sections.name: Employment
sections.why: Connect real responsibilities to the target without changing job titles.
sections.example: Describe an observed problem, what you did and the outcome you can support.

sections.name: Certifications
sections.why: Use exact credential names and distinguish certificates from licences.
sections.example: Record the issuer and completion date; course completion does not authorize regulated practice.

sections.name: Publications / presentations
sections.why: Give accurate authorship, venue and status.
sections.example: Label a class presentation as a class presentation and a manuscript draft as a draft.

sections.name: Awards
sections.why: Use exact award names, levels and dates.
sections.example: Explain the competition context only where supported; do not invent a percentile.

sections.name: Leadership
sections.why: Show decisions, coordination and accountability.
sections.example: Fictional example: organized the team’s review checklist and documented agreed changes before the handover.

sections.name: Volunteering
sections.why: Describe a real contribution and its context.
sections.example: Fictional example: prepared accessible learning materials and revised them after supervisor feedback.

default.note: Use official public aggregate data or clearly labelled synthetic examples; choose a dataset appropriate to the question.

mse.note: UCI SECOM is suitable for the semiconductor-data project; use published property data for materials-selection exercises and verify each dataset’s licence.

physics.note: Use an educational CERN Open Data sample and follow its documentation and reuse conditions.

chemistry.note: PubChem offers public chemical information; choose a relevant property dataset and verify provenance.

biology.note: GBIF public observations require licence, sampling-bias and location-sensitivity checks.

medicine.note: Use openly permitted educational or synthetic data only; many PhysioNet datasets have additional credential and data-use restrictions.

veterinary.note: Use public aggregate surveillance or educational guidance; no animal handling or clinical inference.

environment.note: Follow links to official public climate datasets and inspect their measurement and aggregation documentation.

law.note: Use official legal materials in a clearly specified jurisdiction; this project is not legal advice.

economics.note: Use public aggregate indicators with definitions, licence and reference dates.

finance.note: Use public company filings and clearly labelled educational models; no investment recommendation.
